chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
title: House-breakers 'Old Man River' and 'Ease On Down'
summary: The band's first house-breaker was an 'Old Man River' arrangement largely Metcalf's idea; 'Ease On Down' was a chorus-girl number whose title was misprinted.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: I remember one flagwaver, I've forgotten the name of the thing, that you never recorded.
That really brought the house down.

Well, we had about seven or eight house-breakers. Well, his "Old Man River" was the first one we had. And I attribute the idea to Louis Metcalf, his "Old Man River," because... It was just an arrangement gotten together from the band. But most of the ideas was Louis Metcalf on "Old Man River." And as we went along, we changed it four or five different times. And they even had a vocal in there on it, as part of the arrangement.
Yeah. Rex Stewart was in the band then.
Yeah, that was much later. Then, what about "Ease On
Down." Wasn't that a big number?

That was a... Well, I wouldn't say that was a house-breaker. Oh, it got its applause, all right. But we used that mostly when we played in theatre for the chorus girls to dance by. That was a chorus number, you know. That's the way we used it most of the time. That was a swingin' number, yes indeed. "Ease On Down." It was "Case On Down" on the record.
Well, they couldn't read Russell's handwriting, which was very small.
Well, yeah, it was misspelled "E-a-s-e" when it should have been "C-a-s-e."
It should have been "E-a-s-e" but it was "C-a-s-e."
Well, it looked like a "C" apparently, and the people who did the graphics put it out as that. But it was really "Ease on Down."
Because it came out as "Case On Dawn." Which meant, obviously, nothing. Whereas "Ease On Down"...
